વાઇવા પ્રશ્નો
1. થર્મોડાયનેમિક્સનો પ્રથમ નિયમ જણાવો અને closed system માટે તેનું ગાણિતિક સ્વરૂપ આપો.

ઊર્જા ઉત્પન્ન કે નષ્ટ થઈ શકતી નથી, ફક્ત રૂપાંતરિત થાય. closed system માટે Q − W = ΔU + Δ(KE) + Δ(PE), અને closed સ્થિર system માટે Q − W = ΔU.

2. Internal energy શું છે? તેનો ફક્ત ફેરફાર જ કેમ ગણાય છે?

Internal energy એ system ના molecular kinetic તથા potential energy નો સરવાળો છે. તેની નિરપેક્ષ કિંમત મનસ્વી reference state પર આધાર રાખે, જે કોઈ energy balance ને અસર કરતી નથી, તેથી ફક્ત states વચ્ચેના તફાવત વપરાય છે.

3. Enthalpy ની વ્યાખ્યા આપો અને flow processes માટે તે કેમ વપરાય છે તે સમજાવો.

H = U + P V. વહેતા fluid માટે surroundings તેને boundary પાર ધકેલવા flow work P V પણ કરે છે; તેને U સાથે જૂથ કરવાથી H મળે, તેથી steady-flow equation માં અલગ flow-work પદ વગર h આવે. એટલે જ steam tables h આપે છે.

4. Gas માટે c_p એ c_v કરતાં મોટું કેમ હોય છે?

અચળ volume પર કોઈ work થતું નથી, તેથી આખી heat internal energy વધારે. અચળ pressure પર gas expand થઈને work P Δv પણ કરે છે, તેથી એટલા જ temperature વધારા માટે વધુ heat જોઈએ. ideal gas માટે c_p − c_v = R.

5. Steady-flow energy equation લખો અને તેની assumptions જણાવો.

q − w_s = (h₂ − h₁) + ½(c₂² − c₁²) + g(z₂ − z₁). Assumptions: steady state, એક inlet તથા એક outlet, દરેક section પર સરખી properties, કોઈ reaction નહીં, અને ઘણી વાર kinetic તથા potential energy ના ફેરફાર નગણ્ય.

6. Non-flow તથા flow પ્રક્રિયા વચ્ચે ભેદ આપો, દરેકનું એક ઉદાહરણ આપો.

Non-flow પ્રક્રિયામાં નિશ્ચિત mass system માં રહે છે અને boundary પાર mass જતું નથી (closed cylinder માં ગરમ થતો gas, Q − W = ΔU). Flow પ્રક્રિયામાં mass સતત અંદર આવે તથા બહાર જાય (compressor, turbine, nozzle) અને સમીકરણ internal energy ને બદલે enthalpy વાપરે.

7. Cyclic પ્રક્રિયા માટે Q_net = W_net સાબિત કરો.

Cycle system ને પ્રારંભિક state પર પાછું લાવે છે, તેથી ΔU = 0. પ્રથમ નિયમ Q − W = ΔU પરથી Q_net = W_net મળે: ચોખ્ખી અપાયેલી heat ચોખ્ખા આપેલા work જેટલી.

8. પહેલા પ્રકારની perpetual-motion machine શું છે?

એવી machine જે કોઈ ઊર્જા લીધા વગર સતત work આપે. પ્રથમ નિયમ તેને નિષેધે છે કારણ કે ઊર્જાનો હિસાબ કદી બેસી શકે નહીં.

  1. થર્મોડાયનેમિક્સનો પ્રથમ નિયમ જણાવો. તેને (i) closed system, (ii) closed સ્થિર system, (iii) cyclic પ્રક્રિયા માટે લખો. (4marks)
  2. Internal energy તથા enthalpy ની વ્યાખ્યા આપો. H = U + P V સંબંધ મેળવો અને flow processes માં enthalpy કેમ આવે તે સમજાવો. (4marks)
  3. Gas માટે c_p એ c_v કરતાં મોટું કેમ છે તે સમજાવો. ideal gas માટે c_p − c_v = R દર્શાવો. (4marks)
  4. એક inlet તથા એક outlet વાળા control volume માટે steady-flow energy equation મેળવો અને બધી assumptions સ્પષ્ટ લખો. (4marks)
  5. Non-flow તથા flow પ્રક્રિયા વચ્ચે ભેદ આપો. દરેકના પ્રથમ નિયમનું સમીકરણ લખો અને દરેકના બે ઉદાહરણ આપો. (4marks)
  6. 0.5 kg હવા દૃઢ પાત્રમાં 27 °C થી 227 °C સુધી ગરમ કરાય છે. W, ΔU તથા Q ગણો. c_v = 0.718 kJ/kg·K લો. (4marks)
  7. 2 kg હવા 400 K પર 1.5 bar થી 0.5 bar સુધી isothermal રીતે expand થાય છે. થયેલું work તથા transfer થયેલી heat શોધો. R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. (4marks)
  8. 300 K પરની 1 kg હવા 5 bar સુધી adiabatic તથા reversible રીતે compress થાય છે. અંતિમ temperature તથા work input શોધો. γ = 1.4, c_v = 0.718 kJ/kg·K લો. (4marks)
  9. Air compressor માં 1 bar, 300 K પર આવે છે અને 6 bar, 480 K પર નીકળે છે. Mass flow 0.05 kg/s, heat loss 3 kW, c_p = 1.005 kJ/kg·K. Shaft power ગણો. (4marks)
  10. Steam insulated nozzle માં 3 082 kJ/kg પર આવે છે અને 2 902 kJ/kg પર નીકળે છે. Inlet velocity 40 m/s હોય તો exit velocity શોધો. (4marks)
  11. ideal gas માટે c_p = 1.005 તથા R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. c_v તથા γ શોધો, અને 2 kg ને અચળ pressure પર 100 K ગરમ કરતાં ΔH, ΔU તથા W ગણો. (4marks)
  12. થર્મોડાયનેમિક્સના પ્રથમ નિયમની મર્યાદાઓ જણાવો અને બીજો નિયમ કેમ જરૂરી છે તે સમજાવો. (4marks)

2. Notes
2.1 • Statement of the first law

Definition / principle

The first law of thermodynamics states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only converted from one form to another. For a closed system that changes from state 1 to state 2, the heat supplied minus the work done equals the change of total energy: Q − W = ΔE.

Detailed theory and conditions

The law is a statement about the accounting, not about the mechanism. It says the books must balance: whatever crosses the boundary as heat either leaves as work or stays inside as a rise of internal, kinetic and potential energy. It therefore forbids a machine that produces work with no energy input (a perpetual-motion machine of the first kind), and it makes internal energy a property with a definite value at every state.

For a closed, stationary system the kinetic and potential terms are zero and the law reduces to the form used in almost every numerical: Q − W = ΔU. When an ideal gas is the system, ΔU = m cv ΔT, so the temperature change follows from the heat and work alone, whatever the path.

Equations and notation

Q−W=ΔU+ΔKE+ΔPE
Q−W=ΔU
δQ−δW=dU

Key points and data

  • Sign convention used here: heat added to the system is positive, work done by the system is positive. State the convention before substituting numbers.
  • Cyclic process: ΔU = 0, so Qnet = Wnet for the cycle.
  • Adiabatic: Q = 0, so W = −ΔU: the work comes out of the internal energy.
  • Perpetual motion of the first kind is a machine giving work without energy input; the first law makes it impossible.

Qualification

The first law fixes only the difference Q − W, never Q and W separately, and it says nothing about direction. A process in which heat flows from cold to hot would satisfy it, so the second law is still needed before any real cycle can be analysed.

2.2 • Internal energy, enthalpy and heat capacity

Definition / principle

Internal energy U is the total energy of the molecules of the system — their translational, rotational and vibrational motion plus the energy stored in molecular bonds. Enthalpy H is the combination H = U + P V. Heat capacity is the heat needed to raise the temperature of the system by one degree: C = δQ/dT, and per unit mass c = C/m.

Detailed theory and conditions

Enthalpy looks like an arbitrary grouping, but it is the natural property for a flow process. When a fluid is pushed into a control volume, the surroundings do flow work P V on it; adding that to U gives H, and the steady-flow energy equation then contains h instead of u, with no separate flow-work term. That is why steam tables tabulate h and not u for most engineering work.

Two heat capacities exist because there are two ways to heat a gas. At constant volume the gas cannot expand, so all the heat raises U: cv = (∂u/∂T)v. At constant pressure the gas also does work P Δv while it expands, so more heat is needed for the same temperature rise: cp = (∂h/∂T)p. For an ideal gas the difference is exactly the gas constant, cp − cv = R, and the ratio γ = cp/cv controls every adiabatic process.

Equations and notation

H=U+PV
h=u+Pv
cv=(∂u∂T)v, cp=(∂h∂T)p
cp−cv=R, γ=cpcv

Key points and data

  • U is a state function; absolute U is never needed, only ΔU between two states.
  • Ideal gas: U and H depend on temperature only (Joule's law), so ΔU = m cv ΔT and ΔH = m cp ΔT for every path.
  • Typical values: air cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, cv = 0.718, γ = 1.40; water cp = 4.187 kJ/kg·K; steam cp ≈ 2.1 kJ/kg·K.
  • Solids and liquids: cp ≈ cv ≈ c because they hardly expand, and both U and H are nearly functions of T alone.

Qualification

Heat capacity is not constant. For real gases it rises with temperature, and for water it peaks near 4 °C. Using a single tabulated c over a wide temperature range is an approximation that must be stated, and near a phase change heat capacity has no meaning at all — the latent heat is used instead.

2.3 • First law for non-flow processes

Definition / principle

A non-flow process is one in which the same fixed mass stays inside the system — filling, heating, expanding a gas in a cylinder. No mass crosses the boundary, so the energy equation is simply Q − W = ΔU, with W = ∫P dV for a reversible path.

Detailed theory and conditions

Four reversible non-flow paths cover almost every question, and each has a characteristic P–V signature. In a constant-volume (isochoric) process no work is done at all, so Q = ΔU = m cv ΔT. In a constant-pressure (isobaric) process the work is P ΔV and the heat supplied equals the enthalpy change, Q = ΔH = m cp ΔT — which is precisely why enthalpy is used for heaters and reactors. In a constant-temperature (isothermal) process of an ideal gas ΔU = 0, so all the heat becomes work. In an adiabatic process Q = 0, so the work comes out of internal energy and the gas cools as it expands.

Equations and notation

W=0, Q=ΔU=mcvΔT
W=PΔV, Q=ΔH=mcpΔT
ΔU=0, W=Q=mRTlnV2V1
Q=0, W=−ΔU=mcv(T1−T2)

Key points and data

  • Isochoric: vertical line on a P–V diagram. Used for a closed vessel being heated.
  • Isobaric: horizontal line. Used for a heater or a piston free to move.
  • Isothermal: rectangular hyperbola P V = constant. Used for slow heat exchange with a large bath.
  • Adiabatic: steeper than the isotherm, P Vγ = constant. Used for a well-insulated compressor or expansion.

Qualification

The formulas W = P ΔV and W = ∫P dV apply to the reversible path. In a real fast expansion the pressure inside the gas is not uniform and the actual work is less; the work must then be taken from the surroundings side or given directly.

2.4 • Steady-flow energy equation

Symbols, model and assumptions

Model: a control volume with one inlet (1) and one outlet (2), working fluid steady, properties uniform across each section. Assumptions: steady state (nothing accumulates), no chemical reaction, negligible change of surface energy, single stream in and out.

  1. Take a control volume between sections 1 and 2. In steady state the mass entering equals the mass leaving, so the same mass m flows in and out.

    ṁin=ṁout=ṁ

  2. Write what enters with the fluid: internal energy, the flow work needed to push it in, kinetic energy and potential energy.

    =m(u1+P1v1)+12mc21+mgz1

  3. Group u + P v, which is the definition of enthalpy. This is the step that removes flow work from the equation.

    u+Pv=h

  4. Write what leaves in the same way, at section 2.

    =m(h2+12c22+gz2)

  5. Apply the first law to the control volume: heat in minus work out equals the energy that left minus the energy that entered. In steady state there is no change of stored energy inside, so the accumulation is zero.

    Q−Ws=out−in

  6. Substitute the two groups and divide by the mass flow, giving the equation in the form used for compressors, turbines and nozzles.

    Q−Ws=m[(h2−h1)+12(c22−c21)+g(z2−z1)]

Result

q−ws=(h2−h1)+12(c22−c21)+g(z2−z1)
2.5 • Forms of work: displacement, flow and shaft

Definition / principle

Work is energy in transit across a boundary under the action of a force. Three forms dominate chemical engineering: displacement work W = ∫P dV, done when a boundary moves against pressure; flow work P V, done by the surroundings to push fluid into or out of a control volume; and shaft work W = 2π N T, delivered through a rotating shaft.

Detailed theory and conditions

The distinction matters because only displacement and shaft work appear as W in the first law; flow work is never written separately — it is absorbed into enthalpy precisely so that the equation stays short. A student who adds a flow-work term to the steady-flow equation is counting the same energy twice.

Sign follows the boundary, not the machine. Work done by the system on the surroundings is positive here, so an expanding gas does positive work and a compressor that consumes work reports a negative W. In an electrical heater the work is negative and the heat supplied is positive, both crossing the same boundary — which is why the account still balances.

Equations and notation

W=∫P dV
Wflow=PV
Ws=2πNT

Key points and data

  • Displacement work is the area under the process curve on a P–V diagram.
  • Flow work P V is not a separate term once enthalpy is used: h = u + P v already contains it.
  • Shaft work is what a pump, compressor, turbine or stirrer delivers; it is positive when the shaft delivers work to the surroundings.
  • Electrical and magnetic work also cross the boundary without a moving part and must be counted in W.

Qualification

The integral ∫P dV gives the work only when the path is reversible, because only then is the pressure inside the gas the same as the pressure at the boundary. For free expansion into vacuum the external pressure is zero, so no work is done even though the gas expands.

2.6 • Relation between c_p and c_v for an ideal gas

Symbols, model and assumptions

Model: one mole of an ideal gas, P V = R T, heated through the same temperature rise twice — once at constant volume, once at constant pressure. Assumptions: ideal gas, no change of kinetic or potential energy, reversible heating.

  1. Heat one mole at constant volume by dT. No work is done, so all the heat raises internal energy and defines c_v.

    δQv=dU=cv dT

  2. Heat one mole at constant pressure by the same dT. Now the gas also does work P dV, so the heat supplied must cover both the internal energy and that work.

    δQp=dU+P dV=cp dT

  3. Subtract the constant-volume result from the constant-pressure result.

    (cp−cv) dT=P dV

  4. Differentiate the ideal-gas law P V = R T at constant pressure, so that P dV can be replaced.

    P dV=R dT

  5. Substitute and cancel dT from both sides to obtain Mayer's relation.

    cp−cv=R

  6. Divide by c_v to get the ratio that controls adiabatic pressure–volume behaviour.

    γ=cpcv

Result

cp−cv=R
Solved numericals and practicals
Work and heat in a closed cylinder of gas

Given

0.5 kg of air is heated in a rigid closed vessel from 27 °C to 227 °C. Take c_v = 0.718 kJ/kg·K.

Find

Work done, heat supplied and change of internal energy.

Formula

W=0
Q=ΔU=mcvΔT

Substitution and calculation

ΔT = 227 − 27 = 200 K. ΔU = 0.5 × 0.718 × 200 = 71.8 kJ. Since W = 0, Q = 71.8 kJ.

Final answer with units

W = 0; ΔU = 71.8 kJ; Q = 71.8 kJ (heat supplied to the air).

Validity check

A rigid vessel cannot change volume, so no displacement work is possible; every joule of heat must appear as internal energy. 0.5 × 0.718 × 200 is the right order for a 200 K rise of half a kilogram of air.

Isothermal expansion of air

Given

2 kg of air expands reversibly and isothermally at 400 K from 1.5 bar to 0.5 bar. R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K.

Find

Work done, heat transferred and change of internal energy.

Formula

W=mRTlnP1P2
ΔU=0⇒Q=W

Substitution and calculation

W = 2 × 0.287 × 400 × ln(1.5/0.5) = 229.6 × ln 3 = 229.6 × 1.0986 = 252.3 kJ.

Final answer with units

W = 252.3 kJ by the air; Q = 252.3 kJ absorbed; ΔU = 0.

Validity check

Pressure falls by a factor of three, so the volume triples and the work is mRT ln 3. ΔU = 0 is the signature of an isothermal ideal-gas process: the whole heat input leaves as work.

Adiabatic compression of air

Given

1 kg of air at 300 K and 1 bar is compressed adiabatically and reversibly to 5 bar. γ = 1.4, c_v = 0.718 kJ/kg·K.

Find

Final temperature, work input and change of internal energy.

Formula

T2T1=(P2P1)γ−1γ
Q=0⇒W=−ΔU

Substitution and calculation

(γ−1)/γ = 0.4/1.4 = 0.2857. T₂ = 300 × (5)^0.2857 = 300 × 1.584 = 475.1 K. ΔU = 1 × 0.718 × (475.1 − 300) = 125.7 kJ. W = −125.7 kJ, i.e. 125.7 kJ of work is put in.

Final answer with units

T₂ = 475 K; work input = 125.7 kJ/kg; ΔU = +125.7 kJ/kg.

Validity check

Adiabatic compression always heats the gas: 300 K to 475 K for a fivefold pressure rise is the standard result, and because Q = 0 the work input must equal the internal-energy rise exactly. The negative sign of W follows the convention that work done by the gas is positive.

Steady-flow compressor

Given

Air enters a compressor at 1 bar, 300 K with negligible velocity and leaves at 6 bar, 480 K. Mass flow 0.05 kg/s. Heat loss from the casing 3 kW. c_p = 1.005 kJ/kg·K.

Find

Shaft power required, and the error made by neglecting the kinetic energy.

Formula

Q−Ws=ṁ[(h2−h1)+12(c22−c21)]
Δh=cp(T2−T1)

Substitution and calculation

Δh = 1.005 × (480 − 300) = 180.9 kJ/kg. With Q = −3 kW (heat lost) and KE neglected: −3 − W_s = 0.05 × 180.9 = 9.045 ⇒ W_s = −12.05 kW. The negative sign means 12.05 kW of shaft power must be supplied.

Final answer with units

Shaft power = 12.05 kW input. Kinetic energy is negligible only if the exit velocity is small; at 50 m/s it would add ½c² = 1.25 kJ/kg, about 0.7 %.

Validity check

For 0.05 kg/s and 180 K rise the gas alone needs 9 kW; adding the 3 kW lost as heat gives about 12 kW, which is the right order for a small compressor. Heat loss increases the power needed, as the sign of Q shows.

Heat capacity relation for an ideal gas

Given

For a certain ideal gas c_p = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. 2 kg of the gas is heated at constant pressure through 100 K.

Find

c_v, γ, ΔH, ΔU and the work done.

Formula

cv=cp−R
γ=cpcv
W=mRΔT

Substitution and calculation

c_v = 1.005 − 0.287 = 0.718 kJ/kg·K. γ = 1.005/0.718 = 1.40. ΔH = 2 × 1.005 × 100 = 201.0 kJ. ΔU = 2 × 0.718 × 100 = 143.6 kJ. W = 2 × 0.287 × 100 = 57.4 kJ.

Final answer with units

c_v = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, γ = 1.40; ΔH = 201.0 kJ; ΔU = 143.6 kJ; W = 57.4 kJ; Q = ΔH = 201.0 kJ.

Validity check

The two routes must agree: Q = ΔU + W = 143.6 + 57.4 = 201.0 kJ, which equals ΔH. That agreement is the definition H = U + P V showing up numerically, and it is the quickest check in any constant-pressure problem.

Nozzle: converting enthalpy into velocity

Given

Steam enters a well-insulated nozzle at 10 bar, 320 °C with velocity 40 m/s and leaves at 3 bar. The inlet enthalpy is 3 082 kJ/kg and the exit enthalpy 2 902 kJ/kg.

Find

Exit velocity and the mass flow needed for 0.5 kg/s of steam to give a thrust.

Formula

h1+12c21=h2+12c22
c2=√2(h1−h2)+c21

Substitution and calculation

h₁ − h₂ = 180 kJ/kg = 180 000 J/kg. Then c₂² = 2 × 180 000 + 40² = 360 000 + 1 600 = 361 600 ⇒ c₂ = 601.3 m/s.

Final answer with units

c₂ ≈ 601 m/s (the 1 600 term is only 0.4 % of the total, so inlet velocity is usually neglected). For 0.5 kg/s the momentum change is 0.5 × 601 ≈ 300 N of thrust.

Validity check

Nozzles are adiabatic and do no shaft work, so the whole enthalpy drop becomes kinetic energy — 180 kJ/kg giving about 600 m/s is the standard order for steam. Note the unit conversion: kJ/kg must be multiplied by 1 000 to give m²/s².

The energy account of a closed system

Same two states, two paths: Q and W differ, ΔU does not

Steady-flow energy equation across a control volume

Heat capacity at constant volume and at constant pressure

First law forms

RelationFormula and notes
Closed systemQ − W = ΔU (stationary); Q − W = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE (general)
Heat in and work out are positive in this course.
Steady flowq − w_s = (h₂ − h₁) + ½(c₂² − c₁²) + g(z₂ − z₁)
One inlet, one outlet, properties uniform at each section.
Cycle∮dU = 0 ⇒ Q_net = W_net
ΔU of a complete cycle is zero.

Properties and heat capacity

RelationFormula and notes
EnthalpyH = U + P V; h = u + P v
h replaces u in every flow equation, with no flow-work term.
Ideal gasΔU = m c_v ΔT; ΔH = m c_p ΔT; c_p − c_v = R; γ = c_p / c_v
True for every path when the gas is ideal.
Non-flow workW = ∫P dV (reversible); constant P: W = P ΔV; constant V: W = 0
Valid for a reversible path only.
Isothermal and adiabaticisothermal: W = mRT ln(V₂/V₁); adiabatic: T₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)^((γ−1)/γ)
Adiabatic also: P V^γ = constant, T V^(γ−1) = constant.
Viva questions
1. State the first law of thermodynamics and give its mathematical form for a closed system.

Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only converted. For a closed system Q − W = ΔU + Δ(KE) + Δ(PE), and for a closed stationary system Q − W = ΔU.

2. What is internal energy? Why is only its change calculated?

Internal energy is the sum of the molecular kinetic and potential energies of the system. Its absolute value depends on an arbitrary reference state, which does not affect any energy balance, so only differences between states are used.

3. Define enthalpy and explain why it is used for flow processes.

H = U + P V. For a flowing fluid the surroundings also do flow work P V to push it across the boundary; grouping that with U gives H, so the steady-flow equation contains h with no separate flow-work term. That is why steam tables give h.

4. Why is c_p greater than c_v for a gas?

At constant volume no work is done, so all the heat raises internal energy. At constant pressure the gas also expands and does work P Δv, so extra heat is needed for the same temperature rise. For an ideal gas c_p − c_v = R.

5. Write the steady-flow energy equation and state its assumptions.

q − w_s = (h₂ − h₁) + ½(c₂² − c₁²) + g(z₂ − z₁). Assumptions: steady state, one inlet and one outlet, uniform properties at each section, no reaction, and changes of kinetic and potential energy often neglected.

6. Distinguish between a non-flow and a flow process with one example each.

In a non-flow process a fixed mass stays in the system and no mass crosses the boundary (gas heated in a closed cylinder, Q − W = ΔU). In a flow process mass enters and leaves continuously (compressor, turbine, nozzle) and the equation uses enthalpy instead of internal energy.

7. Show that Q_net = W_net for a cyclic process.

A cycle returns the system to its initial state, so ΔU = 0. The first law Q − W = ΔU then gives Q_net = W_net: the net heat supplied equals the net work delivered.

8. What is a perpetual-motion machine of the first kind?

A machine that would deliver work continuously with no energy input. The first law forbids it because the energy account could never balance.

  1. State the first law of thermodynamics. Express it for (i) a closed system, (ii) a closed stationary system, (iii) a cyclic process. (4marks)
  2. Define internal energy and enthalpy. Derive the relation H = U + P V and explain why enthalpy appears in flow processes. (4marks)
  3. Explain why c_p is greater than c_v for a gas. Show that c_p − c_v = R for an ideal gas. (4marks)
  4. Derive the steady-flow energy equation for a control volume with one inlet and one outlet, stating all assumptions clearly. (4marks)
  5. Distinguish between a non-flow and a flow process. Write the first-law equation for each and give two examples of each. (4marks)
  6. 0.5 kg of air is heated in a rigid vessel from 27 °C to 227 °C. Calculate W, ΔU and Q. Take c_v = 0.718 kJ/kg·K. (4marks)
  7. 2 kg of air expands isothermally at 400 K from 1.5 bar to 0.5 bar. Find the work done and the heat transferred. R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. (4marks)
  8. 1 kg of air at 300 K is compressed adiabatically and reversibly to 5 bar. Find the final temperature and the work input. Take γ = 1.4, c_v = 0.718 kJ/kg·K. (4marks)
  9. Air enters a compressor at 1 bar, 300 K and leaves at 6 bar, 480 K. Mass flow 0.05 kg/s, heat loss 3 kW, c_p = 1.005 kJ/kg·K. Calculate the shaft power. (4marks)
  10. Steam enters an insulated nozzle at 3 082 kJ/kg and leaves at 2 902 kJ/kg. If the inlet velocity is 40 m/s, find the exit velocity. (4marks)
  11. For an ideal gas c_p = 1.005 and R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. Find c_v and γ, and calculate ΔH, ΔU and W when 2 kg is heated at constant pressure through 100 K. (4marks)

3. નોટ્સ
3.1 • pure fluid નું PVT વર્તન

વ્યાખ્યા / સિદ્ધાંત

PVT વર્તન એ પદાર્થના pressure, volume તથા temperature વચ્ચેનો સંબંધ છે. pure fluid માટે ત્રણમાંથી ફક્ત બે સ્વતંત્ર હોય છે (single phase માટે F = 2), તેથી કોઈપણ બે પરથી state પૂરી રીતે નક્કી થાય અને ત્રીજું equation of state, table કે diagram પરથી મળે.

વિગતવાર Theory તથા Conditions

સંપૂર્ણ વર્તન ત્રિ-પરિમાણીય surface છે. Engineer તે surface દોરતા નથી; તેના બે દૃશ્ય લે છે. P–V diagram (અચળ temperature ના slice) પરિચિત isotherms, તેમના સપાટ condensation plateau તથા saturation dome દર્શાવે છે. P–T diagram (phase boundaries નું projection) ત્રણ પ્રદેશ — solid, liquid, vapour — દર્શાવે છે, જે fusion, sublimation તથા vapour-pressure curves થી અલગ પડે છે અને triple point પર મળે છે.

P–T diagram પરની દરેક રેખાનો ચોક્કસ અર્થ છે. vapour-pressure રેખા પર liquid તથા vapour સાથે રહે છે, તેથી P = 2 અને F = 1: temperature પસંદ કરતાં pressure નિશ્ચિત થાય. એક જ phase વાળા પ્રદેશમાં F = 2 અને બંને પસંદ કરી શકાય. triple point પર F = 0 અને પ્રકૃતિ બંને નિશ્ચિત કરે છે. critical point ઉપર કોઈ boundary જ નથી, અને તે પદાર્થને supercritical fluid કહે છે.

સમીકરણો તથા Notation

PV=ZnRT
(∂P∂V)T=0
Pr=PPc

મુખ્ય મુદ્દા તથા data

  • Triple point of water: 0.01 °C and 0.006 11 bar — ice, water and vapour coexist.
  • Critical point of water: 374.15 °C and 221.2 bar; above it no amount of pressure will liquefy steam.
  • Critical point of CO₂: 31.0 °C and 73.8 bar — why CO₂ is a convenient supercritical solvent.
  • Below the triple point a solid sublimes directly to vapour; that is why ice evaporates in a freezer without melting.

નોંધ

P–V diagram એક સમયે ફક્ત એક temperature દર્શાવે છે; P–T diagram phase boundaries દર્શાવે છે પણ volume નહીં. એકલું કોઈ પણ પૂરતું નથી — equation of state કે table ત્રીજું variable આપે છે, એટલે જ steam tables v, u, h તથા s સાથે આપે છે.

3.2 • P–T diagram, triple point તથા critical point

વ્યાખ્યા / સિદ્ધાંત

P–T diagram pure substance ની phase boundaries ને pressure–temperature plane માં દર્શાવે છે. ત્રણ curves triple point પર મળે છે: sublimation curve (solid–vapour), fusion curve (solid–liquid) અને vapour-pressure curve (liquid–vapour), જે critical point પર પૂરી થાય છે.

વિગતવાર Theory તથા Conditions

દરેક curve એક degree of freedom ધરાવે છે. vapour-pressure curve પર liquid તથા vapour સાથે રહે, તેથી F = C − P + 2 = 1 − 2 + 2 = 1: એક પસંદગી (જેમ કે boiler નું pressure) ઉકળવાનું temperature નિશ્ચિત કરે. triple point પર ત્રણેય phases સાથે રહે, F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0, તેથી પાણી માટે તે બરાબર 0.01 °C તથા 0.006 11 bar પર થાય અને બદલી શકાય નહીં.

પાણીની fusion curve પાછળ તરફ ઢળે છે (ઋણ ઢોળાવ), જે અસામાન્ય છે: બરફ પર pressure વધારતાં તેનું melting point ઘટે છે, કારણ કે બરફ પાણી કરતાં ઓછા density નો છે. એટલે જ સ્કેટર ના બ્લેડ નીચે પાતળો પડ ઓગળે છે. લગભગ દરેક બીજા પદાર્થની fusion curve આગળ તરફ ઢળે છે. vapour-pressure curve critical point પર પૂરી થાય; તેની પાર liquid તથા gas અલગ ઓળખી શકાતા નથી અને supercritical fluid શબ્દ વપરાય છે.

સમીકરણો તથા Notation

lnP2P1=−ΔHvapR(1T2−1T1)
F=1
F=0

મુખ્ય મુદ્દા તથા data

  • Water: triple point 0.01 °C, 0.006 11 bar; critical point 374.15 °C, 221.2 bar.
  • CO₂: triple point −56.6 °C, 5.18 bar — solid CO₂ (dry ice) sublimes at atmospheric pressure, it never melts.
  • Clausius–Clapeyron gives the slope of the vapour-pressure curve and is used to estimate boiling points at other pressures.
  • Supercritical CO₂ (above 31 °C, 73.8 bar) is used for decaffeination and dry-cleaning because it is a dense, tunable solvent.

નોંધ

P–T diagram volume વિશે કે દરેક phase કેટલી છે તે વિશે કંઈ કહેતું નથી — vapour-pressure રેખા પરનું બિંદુ 1 % vapour કે 99 % vapour હોઈ શકે. તેના માટે P–V diagram કે quality ની કિંમત જોઈએ.

3.3 • ideal gas તથા equation of state

વ્યાખ્યા / સિદ્ધાંત

Ideal gas એ model છે જેમાં molecules નું volume નગણ્ય હોય અને elastic collisions સિવાય એકબીજા પર બળ ન કરે. તેનું equation of state P V = n R T છે, અને gas constant R = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K = હવા માટે 0.287 kJ/kg·K.

વિગતવાર Theory તથા Conditions

આ model એ દરેક વાસ્તવિક fluid ને માપવાનો પાયો છે, અને તેના પરિણામો મોઢે યાદ રાખવા જેવા છે કારણ કે તે મોટાભાગના દાખલા આવરી લે છે. Internal energy તથા enthalpy ફક્ત temperature પર આધાર રાખે છે (Joule's law), તેથી દરેક path માટે ΔU = m cv ΔT અને ΔH = m cp ΔT. અચળ temperature પર P V અચળ; અચળ pressure પર V/T અચળ; અચળ volume પર P/T અચળ.

આ model નીચા pressure તથા ઊંચા temperature પર સચોટ છે, જ્યાં molecules દૂર દૂર હોય અને તેમનું volume તથા attraction ભાગ્યે જ મહત્વનાં રહે. boiling point તથા critical point ની નજીક તે ખૂબ નિષ્ફળ જાય છે, અને ત્યાં જ real-gas corrections જરૂરી થાય. વાસ્તવિક પદાર્થ પર P V = n R T વાપરતાં પહેલાં 'behaves as an ideal gas' assumption હંમેશા લખો.

સમીકરણો તથા Notation

PV=nRT
R=8.314
Vm=22.414 m^3/kmol

મુખ્ય મુદ્દા તથા data

  • Boyle's law (T, n constant): P V = constant.
  • Charles's law (P, n constant): V / T = constant.
  • Gay-Lussac's law (V, n constant): P / T = constant.
  • Always use absolute pressure and absolute temperature in P V = n R T.

નોંધ

કોઈ gas ideal નથી. 300 K તથા 1 bar પર હવા લગભગ 0.1 % જ ideal ની નજીક છે; 10 bar તથા 180 °C પર steam નથી. pressure સાથે અને saturation ની નજીક ભૂલ વધે છે, તેથી critical point ની નજીક P V = n R T થી મળેલો જવાબ compressibility chart સાથે ચકાસવો જોઈએ.

3.4 • ideal-gas પ્રક્રિયાઓ: અચળ V, P, T, adiabatic તથા polytropic

વ્યાખ્યા / સિદ્ધાંત

Ideal-gas process એ એવો રસ્તો છે જેમાં P, V તથા T વચ્ચેનો એક સંબંધ જળવાય. પાંચ વપરાય છે: અચળ volume (isochoric), અચળ pressure (isobaric), અચળ temperature (isothermal), heat transfer વગર (adiabatic) અને સામાન્ય polytropic રસ્તો P Vn = અચળ, જેમાં પહેલા ચાર તેના ખાસ કિસ્સા છે.

વિગતવાર Theory તથા Conditions

polytropic સંબંધ આખા વિષયની ચાવી છે. n = 0 મૂકતાં P = અચળ (isobaric), n = 1 મૂકતાં P V = અચળ (isothermal, ideal gas), n = γ મૂકતાં adiabatic રસ્તો અને n → ∞ મૂકતાં V = અચળ (isochoric) મળે. તેથી work માટેનું એક જ સૂત્ર W = m R (T₁ − T₂)/(n − 1) isothermal સિવાય દરેક કિસ્સો આવરી લે છે; ત્યાં denominator શૂન્ય થાય તેથી logarithmic સ્વરૂપ વાપરવું પડે.

એક જ બિંદુમાંથી પસાર થતો adiabatic રસ્તો isothermal કરતાં હંમેશા ઢોળાવવાળો હોય છે, કારણ કે γ > 1. એટલે જ adiabatic રીતે expand થતાં gas ઠંડું થાય — work તેની internal energy માંથી આવે — અને એટલે જ compressor ગરમ થાય. વાસ્તવિક compressor ના suction તથા discharge stroke દરમિયાન pressure લગભગ અચળ volume પર ઘટે તથા વધે, એટલે indicator diagram ના છેડા ગોળ હોય છે, સીધા ઊભા નહીં.

સમીકરણો તથા Notation

PVn=c
W=mRTlnV2V1
T2T1=(P2P1)γ−1γ
Q=mcv(T2−T1)γ−nγ−1

મુખ્ય મુદ્દા તથા data

  • n = 0 isobaric, n = 1 isothermal, n = γ adiabatic, n = ∞ isochoric; real compression often has n ≈ 1.2–1.35.
  • Adiabatic: Q = 0, so W = −ΔU and the gas cools on expansion.
  • Isothermal: ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so W = Q.
  • Watch the sign: work done by the gas is positive; a compressor that consumes work reports W negative.

નોંધ

W = m R (T₁ − T₂)/(n − 1) સૂત્ર n → 1 આસપાસ નિષ્ફળ જાય છે, ત્યાં 0/0 થાય; તેથી ત્યાં logarithmic સ્વરૂપ વાપરો. તે આખા temperature ગાળામાં c અચળ હોવાનું પણ ધારે છે, જે મોટા ગાળા માટે તથા CO₂ જેવા gases માટે નબળું assumption છે.

3.5 • adiabatic સંબંધ P V^γ = અચળ

સંકેતો, Model તથા Assumptions

Model: સંપૂર્ણ insulated cylinder માં ideal gas, reversible તથા adiabatic રીતે compress થાય છે. Assumptions: cv તથા cp અચળ હોય તેવો ideal gas, reversible path, heat transfer નહીં (Q = 0), kinetic કે potential energy નો ફેરફાર નહીં.

  1. closed system માટે પ્રથમ નિયમ થી શરૂ કરો અને adiabatic રસ્તા માટે Q = 0 મૂકો.

    −P dV=mcv dT

  2. એ જ mass માટે ideal-gas law લખો અને અચળ mass પર તેનું differential લો.

    P dV+V dP=mR dT

  3. બંને સમીકરણો વચ્ચે dT દૂર કરો જેથી ફક્ત P તથા V વચ્ચેનો સંબંધ મળે.

    P dV+V dP=−RcvP dV

  4. P dV ના પદ એકઠાં કરો. R/c_v = γ − 1 વાપરો, જે c_p − c_v = R તથા γ = c_p/c_v પરથી મળે.

    V dP=−γP dV

  5. Variables અલગ કરો જેથી P સાથે dP અને V સાથે dV રહે.

    dPP=−γdVV

  6. γ અચળ રાખીને state 1 તથા 2 વચ્ચે integrate કરો.

    lnP2P1=−γlnV2V1

  7. બંને બાજુ exponential લો અને પ્રમાણભૂત સ્વરૂપમાં ગોઠવો.

    PVγ=const

પરિણામ

PVγ=c
3.6 • વાસ્તવિક gases માટે equations of state

વ્યાખ્યા / સિદ્ધાંત

વાસ્તવિક gas P V = n R T થી વિચલિત થાય છે કારણ કે તેના molecules નું ચોક્કસ volume હોય છે અને એકબીજાને આકર્ષે છે. વિચલન compressibility factor Z = P V / n R T થી મપાય છે, જે ideal gas માટે 1 થાય અને pressure વધતાં કે temperature critical temperature ની નજીક આવતાં 1 થી દૂર જાય.

વિગતવાર Theory તથા Conditions

Z curve નો આકાર બે corrections સમજાવે છે. મધ્યમ pressure પર molecules વચ્ચેનું attraction તેમને ideal કરતાં નજીક ખેંચે છે, તેથી volume નાનું થાય અને Z 1 થી નીચે જાય. ઊંચા pressure પર molecules નું પોતાનું volume ઓછી ખાલી જગ્યા છોડે છે, તેથી Z 1 થી ઉપર જાય. ખૂબ નીચા pressure પર બંને અસરો જતી રહે અને Z → 1 થાય, એટલે જ atmospheric conditions ની નજીક ideal-gas law ખૂબ સારી કામ કરે છે.

વ્યવહારમાં ત્રણ સાધનો વપરાય છે. Van der Waals equation (P + a/V²)(V − b) = R T બંને corrections સ્પષ્ટ લાગુ કરે છે અને પછીના દરેક cubic equation નો પાયો છે. virial equation Z = 1 + B/V + C/V² + … Z ને volume ની ઘાતોમાં વિસ્તારે છે અને તેના coefficients પ્રયોગથી મળે છે. compressibility chart corresponding states ના સિદ્ધાંત વાપરે છે: બધા gases reduced pressure તથા temperature સામે દોરતાં લગભગ એ જ Z curve પાળે છે, તેથી એક જ chart દરેક gas માટે કામ લાગે છે.

સમીકરણો તથા Notation

Z=PVnRT
(P+aV2)(V−b)=RT
Z=1+BV+CV2
a=27R2T2c64Pc

મુખ્ય મુદ્દા તથા data

  • Van der Waals constants: a measures attraction (large for polar gases), b measures molecular volume.
  • Critical constants from a and b: Tc = 8a/(27Rb), Pc = a/(27b²), Vc = 3b.
  • Virial: B is the second virial coefficient, negative at low temperature (attraction dominates) and positive at high temperature.
  • Corresponding states: all gases have Z ≈ 1 when Tr is large, so the chart is used mainly for 0.8 < Tr < 3.

નોંધ

Van der Waals equation ગુણાત્મક છે, સચોટ નથી: તે દરેક gas માટે critical compressibility factor Zc = 3/8 = 0.375 આપે છે, જ્યારે વાસ્તવિક gases લગભગ 0.23 થી 0.29 સુધી હોય છે. તેનો ઉપયોગ વર્તન સમજાવવા તથા cubic equations નો પરિચય આપવા માટે થાય, equipment નું size નક્કી કરવા માટે નહીં.

ઉકેલેલા દાખલા તથા પ્રેક્ટિકલ
ideal-gas law: આપેલી શરતો પર gas નું volume

આપેલ

3 kmol ideal gas 4 bar તથા 320 K પર રખાય છે. R = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K.

શોધો

Gas દ્વારા રોકાયેલું volume.

સૂત્ર

V=nRTP

Substitution તથા Calculation

P = 4 bar = 400 kPa. V = 3 × 8.314 × 320 / 400 = 7 981.4 / 400 = 19.95 m³.

Units સાથે અંતિમ જવાબ

V = 19.95 m³ ≈ 20 m³.

Validity Check

320 K તથા 4 bar પર એક kmol લગભગ 22.4 × (320/273) × (1/4) ≈ 6.6 m³ રોકે, તેથી ત્રણ kmol લગભગ 20 m³ આપે — જવાબ સાચો ક્રમ છે.

PV^γ સંબંધ સાથે adiabatic compression

આપેલ

1 bar તથા 300 K પરની 2 kg હવા 8 bar સુધી adiabatic તથા reversible રીતે compress થાય છે. γ = 1.4, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, c_v = 0.718 kJ/kg·K.

શોધો

અંતિમ temperature, work input તથા heat transfer.

સૂત્ર

T2=T1(P2P1)γ−1γ
W=mR(T1−T2)γ−1

Substitution તથા Calculation

(γ−1)/γ = 0.2857. T₂ = 300 × 8^0.2857 = 300 × 1.811 = 543.3 K. W = 2 × 0.287 × (300 − 543.3)/0.4 = 0.574 × (−243.3)/0.4 = −349.1 kJ. ઋણ ચિહ્ન એટલે 349.1 kJ work આપવું પડે.

Units સાથે અંતિમ જવાબ

T₂ = 543 K; W = −349.1 kJ (work input); Q = 0; ΔU = +349.1 kJ.

Validity Check

ΔU થી ચકાસો: m c_v ΔT = 2 × 0.718 × 243.3 = 349.3 kJ, જે round-off ની અંદર work સાથે મળે — એ જરૂરી છે, કારણ કે Q = 0 એટલે આખું work internal energy બને.

compressibility factor તથા વાસ્તવિક volume

આપેલ

310 K તથા 70 bar પર carbon dioxide. Tc = 304.2 K, Pc = 73.8 bar. આ reduced શરતો પર compressibility chart Z ≈ 0.72 આપે છે. R = 0.1889 kJ/kg·K.

શોધો

Reduced properties, Z, તથા વાસ્તવિક specific volume ની ideal કિંમત સાથે સરખામણી.

સૂત્ર

Tr=TTc
v=ZRTP

Substitution તથા Calculation

T_r = 310/304.2 = 1.019; P_r = 70/73.8 = 0.949. Ideal volume: v_ideal = 0.1889 × 310/7 000 = 8.366 × 10⁻³ m³/kg. Actual: v = 0.72 × 8.366 × 10⁻³ = 6.02 × 10⁻³ m³/kg.

Units સાથે અંતિમ જવાબ

T_r = 1.02, P_r = 0.95, Z = 0.72; v = 6.02 × 10⁻³ m³/kg, ideal કરતાં લગભગ 28 % ઓછું.

Validity Check

Tr ≈ 1 એટલે gas પોતાના critical temperature ની નજીક છે, જ્યાં Z 1 થી ઘણું દૂર હોય; ideal-gas law વાપર્યું હોત તો volume 39 % વધારે આવત. એટલે જ 31 °C ની નજીક CO₂ નબળો ideal gas છે પણ ઉત્તમ dense solvent છે.

એક mole માટે Van der Waals equation

આપેલ

એક mole gas 300 K પર 0.5 L રોકે છે. gas માટે a = 3.592 bar·L²/mol² તથા b = 0.042 67 L/mol. R = 0.083 14 bar·L/mol·K.

શોધો

ideal-gas law તથા Van der Waals equation થી pressure.

સૂત્ર

P=RTV
P=RTV−b−aV2

Substitution તથા Calculation

Ideal: P = 0.083 14 × 300/0.5 = 49.88 bar. Van der Waals: V − b = 0.5 − 0.042 67 = 0.457 33 L. R T/(V − b) = 24.942/0.457 33 = 54.54 bar. a/V² = 3.592/0.25 = 14.37 bar. P = 54.54 − 14.37 = 40.17 bar.

Units સાથે અંતિમ જવાબ

P_ideal = 49.9 bar; P_vdW = 40.2 bar — ideal law લગભગ 24 % વધારે આપે છે.

Validity Check

બંને corrections વિરુદ્ધ દિશામાં ખેંચે છે: volume correction (V − b) pressure વધારે છે, attraction પદ (a/V²) ઘટાડે છે, અને અહીં attraction જીતે છે. આ density પર gas ideal થી ઘણું દૂર છે, જે પ્રતિ mole અડધા લિટર માટે અપેક્ષિત નિષ્કર્ષ છે.

હવાનું polytropic compression

આપેલ

1.5 kg હવા 1 bar, 290 K થી 6 bar સુધી P V^1.25 = અચળ પ્રમાણે compress થાય છે. R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, c_v = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, γ = 1.4.

શોધો

અંતિમ temperature, work input, heat transfer તથા polytropic index ની ચકાસણી.

સૂત્ર

T2=T1(P2P1)n−1n
W=mR(T1−T2)n−1
Q=mcv(T2−T1)γ−nγ−1

Substitution તથા Calculation

(n−1)/n = 0.25/1.25 = 0.2. T₂ = 290 × 6^0.2 = 290 × 1.431 = 415.0 K. W = 1.5 × 0.287 × (290 − 415)/0.25 = 0.4305 × (−125)/0.25 = −215.3 kJ. Q = 1.5 × 0.718 × 125 × (1.4 − 1.25)/0.4 = 1.077 × 125 × 0.375 = −50.5 kJ.

Units સાથે અંતિમ જવાબ

T₂ = 415 K; work input = 215.3 kJ; heat rejected ≈ 50.5 kJ. 1 < n < γ હોવાથી compress થતાં gas ઠંડું પણ થાય છે.

Validity Check

પ્રથમ નિયમ થી ચકાસો: ΔU = m c_v ΔT = 1.5 × 0.718 × 125 = 134.6 kJ. Q − W = −50.5 − (−215.3) = 164.8 kJ, જે ΔU જેટલું હોવું જોઈએ. તફાવત c_v માં round-off નો છે; બરાબર મેળ માટે c_v = R/(γ − 1) = 0.7175 વાપરો.

pure substance નું P–V diagram

P–V diagram પર પાંચ ideal-gas પ્રક્રિયાઓ

generalised compressibility chart

વાસ્તવિક gases કેમ વિચલિત થાય: compressibility factor Z

ideal-gas સંબંધો

RelationFormula and notes
Equation of stateP V = n R T; P v = R T; P V = m R T
Absolute pressure and absolute temperature only.
Gas constantR = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K = 0.287 kJ/kg·K (air); R_u = M R
Molar and specific forms differ by the molar mass.
Standard volume22.414 m³/kmol at 1 atm, 0 °C; 22.71 m³/kmol at 1 bar, 0 °C
Handy for converting a gas flow to a molar flow.

પ્રક્રિયા સંબંધો (ideal gas)

RelationFormula and notes
PolytropicP V^n = c; W = mR(T₁ − T₂)/(n − 1); Q = m c_v (T₂ − T₁)(γ − n)/(γ − 1)
Covers isobaric, isothermal, adiabatic and isochoric as special cases.
Isothermal (n = 1)W = Q = m R T ln(V₂/V₁) = m R T ln(P₁/P₂)
Denominator n − 1 vanishes, so use the logarithmic form.
AdiabaticT₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)^((γ−1)/γ); P V^γ = c; T V^(γ−1) = c
Q = 0, so W = −ΔU = m c_v (T₁ − T₂).

વાસ્તવિક-gas સંબંધો

RelationFormula and notes
Compressibility factorZ = P V / n R T; V = Z n R T / P
Read Z from the chart using Pr and Tr.
Reduced coordinatesP_r = P/P_c; T_r = T/T_c; V_r = V/V_c
Principle of corresponding states: all gases collapse onto one chart.
Van der Waals(P + a/V²)(V − b) = R T; Tc = 8a/(27Rb); Pc = a/(27b²)
Predicts Zc = 3/8 for every gas, so use it qualitatively.
VirialZ = 1 + B/V + C/V² + …
B negative at low T (attraction), positive at high T.
વાઇવા પ્રશ્નો
1. pure fluid નું PVT વર્તન સમજાવો અને કેટલી properties તેની state નક્કી કરે તે જણાવો.

PVT વર્તન એ pressure, volume તથા temperature વચ્ચેનો સંબંધ છે. single phase માં pure fluid માટે ત્રણમાંથી ફક્ત બે સ્વતંત્ર હોય (F = 2), તેથી કોઈપણ બે નિશ્ચિત કરતાં ત્રીજું equation of state કે table દ્વારા નિશ્ચિત થાય.

2. pure substance નું P–V diagram દોરો અને સમજાવો.

Tc થી નીચે isotherms સપાટ plateau દર્શાવે છે જ્યાં liquid તથા vapour સાથે રહે છે. T વધતાં plateau ટૂંકું થાય અને critical point પર અદૃશ્ય થાય. Tc ઉપર isotherm સતત હોય — phase change નહીં. dome બધા plateau ના છેડા જોડે છે.

3. ideal-gas law જણાવો અને તે કઈ શરતોમાં લાગુ પડે તે જણાવો.

P V = n R T. તે નીચા pressure તથા ઊંચા temperature પર લાગુ પડે છે, જ્યાં molecular volume તથા intermolecular attraction નગણ્ય હોય. critical point તથા saturation ની નજીક તે નિષ્ફળ જાય.

4. polytropic process શું છે? n = 0, 1, γ તથા ∞ શું દર્શાવે છે?

P V^n = અચળ પાળતી પ્રક્રિયા. n = 0 isobaric, n = 1 isothermal, n = γ adiabatic અને n → ∞ isochoric. વાસ્તવિક compression માં n સામાન્ય રીતે 1.2 થી 1.35 હોય છે.

5. adiabatic curve isothermal કરતાં ઢોળાવવાળો કેમ હોય છે?

adiabatic રસ્તા પર કોઈ heat અંદર આવતી નથી, તેથી work internal energy માંથી આવે અને gas expand થતાં temperature ઘટે. isothermal રસ્તો heat લઈને T અચળ રાખે. γ > 1 હોવાથી P V^γ = c એ P V = c કરતાં ઝડપથી ઘટે છે.

6. compressibility factor Z ની વ્યાખ્યા આપો અને તે 1 થી ઓછું કે વધુ કેમ હોઈ શકે તે સમજાવો.

Z = P V / n R T. intermolecular attraction પ્રભાવી હોય અને volume ideal કરતાં નાનું હોય ત્યારે 1 થી નીચે; ઊંચા pressure પર molecular volume પ્રભાવી હોય ત્યારે 1 થી ઉપર. P → 0 થતાં Z → 1.

7. Van der Waals equation લખો અને a તથા b નો અર્થ જણાવો.

(P + a/V²)(V − b) = R T. a અચળ intermolecular attraction સુધારે છે અને b molecules દ્વારા રોકાયેલા ચોક્કસ volume માટે.

8. corresponding states નો સિદ્ધાંત શું છે?

બધા gases reduced coordinates Pr = P/Pc તથા Tr = T/Tc માં લખતાં લગભગ એ જ compressibility સંબંધ પાળે છે. તેથી એક generalised chart દરેક gas માટે કામ લાગે, એટલે જ compressibility chart સાર્વત્રિક છે.

  1. P–V તથા P–T diagrams ની મદદથી pure substance નું PVT વર્તન સમજાવો. triple point તથા critical point દર્શાવો. (4marks)
  2. ideal-gas law જણાવો અને તેની મર્યાદાઓ સમજાવો. critical point ની નજીક તે કેમ નિષ્ફળ જાય? (4marks)
  3. ideal gas ની reversible adiabatic પ્રક્રિયા માટે P V^γ = અચળ મેળવો અને assumptions જણાવો. (4marks)
  4. P–V diagram પર પાંચ ideal-gas પ્રક્રિયાઓ દોરો અને દરેક માટે થયેલું work તથા heat આપો. (4marks)
  5. વાસ્તવિક gases નું ideal વર્તનથી વિચલન સમજાવો. Z વ્યાખ્યાયિત કરો અને તે 1 થી ઓછું કે વધુ કેમ હોઈ શકે તે સમજાવો. (4marks)
  6. Van der Waals equation લખો અને તેના constants સમજાવો. નીચા pressure પર તે ideal-gas law માં કેમ ફેરવાય તે દર્શાવો. (4marks)
  7. virial equation લખો અને second virial coefficient નું મહત્વ સમજાવો. (4marks)
  8. generalised compressibility chart શું છે? corresponding states નો સિદ્ધાંત તથા chart વાપરવાની રીત સમજાવો. (4marks)
  9. 3 kmol ideal gas 4 bar તથા 320 K પર છે. તેનું volume ગણો. R = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K. (4marks)
  10. 1 bar, 300 K પરની 2 kg હવા 8 bar સુધી adiabatic તથા reversible રીતે compress થાય છે. T₂ તથા work input શોધો. γ = 1.4, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. (4marks)
  11. 310 K તથા 70 bar પર CO₂ માટે Tc = 304.2 K તથા Pc = 73.8 bar છે. Reduced properties શોધો અને Z = 0.72 વાપરીને specific volume ગણો તથા ideal કિંમત સાથે સરખાવો. (4marks)
  12. 1.5 kg હવા 1 bar, 290 K થી 6 bar સુધી P V^1.25 = અચળ પ્રમાણે compress થાય છે. T₂, work input તથા heat transfer ગણો. (4marks)

3. Notes
3.1 • PVT behaviour of a pure fluid

Definition / principle

The PVT behaviour of a substance is the relationship between its pressure, volume and temperature. For a pure fluid only two of the three are independent (F = 2 for a single phase), so the state is completely fixed by any two of them and the third follows from an equation of state, a table or a diagram.

Detailed theory and conditions

The complete behaviour is a surface in three dimensions. Engineers never draw that surface; they take two views of it. The P–V diagram (at fixed temperature slices) shows the familiar isotherms with their flat condensation plateaus and the saturation dome. The P–T diagram (projecting the phase boundaries) shows three regions — solid, liquid, vapour — separated by the fusion, sublimation and vapour-pressure curves, meeting at the triple point.

Each line on a P–T diagram carries a definite meaning. On the vapour-pressure line liquid and vapour coexist, so P = 2 and F = 1: choosing the temperature fixes the pressure. In the region inside one phase F = 2 and both may be chosen. At the triple point F = 0 and nature fixes both. Above the critical point there is no boundary at all, and the substance is called a supercritical fluid.

Equations and notation

PV=ZnRT
(∂P∂V)T=0
Pr=PPc

Key points and data

  • Triple point of water: 0.01 °C and 0.006 11 bar — ice, water and vapour coexist.
  • Critical point of water: 374.15 °C and 221.2 bar; above it no amount of pressure will liquefy steam.
  • Critical point of CO₂: 31.0 °C and 73.8 bar — why CO₂ is a convenient supercritical solvent.
  • Below the triple point a solid sublimes directly to vapour; that is why ice evaporates in a freezer without melting.

Qualification

The P–V diagram shows only one temperature at a time; the P–T diagram shows the phase boundaries but no volume. Neither alone is enough — an equation of state or a table gives the third variable, which is why steam tables list v, u, h and s together.

3.2 • The P–T diagram, triple point and critical point

Definition / principle

The P–T diagram plots the phase boundaries of a pure substance in the pressure–temperature plane. Three curves meet at the triple point: the sublimation curve (solid–vapour), the fusion curve (solid–liquid) and the vapour-pressure curve (liquid–vapour), which ends at the critical point.

Detailed theory and conditions

Each curve carries one degree of freedom. On the vapour-pressure curve liquid and vapour coexist, so F = C − P + 2 = 1 − 2 + 2 = 1: a single choice (say the pressure of a boiler) fixes the boiling temperature. At the triple point all three phases coexist, F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0, so for water it occurs at exactly 0.01 °C and 0.006 11 bar and cannot be shifted.

The fusion curve of water slopes backwards (negative slope), which is unusual: increasing the pressure on ice lowers its melting point, because ice is less dense than water. That is why a skater's blade melts a thin film under it. For almost every other substance the fusion curve slopes forward. The vapour-pressure curve ends at the critical point; beyond it the liquid and gas are indistinguishable and the term supercritical fluid is used.

Equations and notation

lnP2P1=−ΔHvapR(1T2−1T1)
F=1
F=0

Key points and data

  • Water: triple point 0.01 °C, 0.006 11 bar; critical point 374.15 °C, 221.2 bar.
  • CO₂: triple point −56.6 °C, 5.18 bar — solid CO₂ (dry ice) sublimes at atmospheric pressure, it never melts.
  • Clausius–Clapeyron gives the slope of the vapour-pressure curve and is used to estimate boiling points at other pressures.
  • Supercritical CO₂ (above 31 °C, 73.8 bar) is used for decaffeination and dry-cleaning because it is a dense, tunable solvent.

Qualification

The P–T diagram says nothing about volume or about how much of each phase is present — a point on the vapour-pressure line could be 1 % vapour or 99 % vapour. The P–V diagram or a quality value is needed for that.

3.3 • Ideal gas and the equation of state

Definition / principle

An ideal gas is a model in which molecules have negligible volume and exert no forces on one another except during elastic collisions. Its equation of state is P V = n R T, and it defines the gas constant R = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K = 0.287 kJ/kg·K for air.

Detailed theory and conditions

The model is the baseline against which every real fluid is judged, and its consequences are worth memorising because they cover most numericals. Internal energy and enthalpy depend on temperature only (Joule's law), so ΔU = m cv ΔT and ΔH = m cp ΔT for every path. At constant temperature P V is constant; at constant pressure V/T is constant; at constant volume P/T is constant.

The model is accurate at low pressure and high temperature, where molecules are far apart and their own volume and attraction hardly matter. It fails badly near the boiling point and near the critical point, which is exactly where real-gas corrections are needed. Always state the assumption 'behaves as an ideal gas' before using P V = n R T on a real substance.

Equations and notation

PV=nRT
R=8.314
Vm=22.414 m^3/kmol

Key points and data

  • Boyle's law (T, n constant): P V = constant.
  • Charles's law (P, n constant): V / T = constant.
  • Gay-Lussac's law (V, n constant): P / T = constant.
  • Always use absolute pressure and absolute temperature in P V = n R T.

Qualification

No gas is ideal. Air at 300 K and 1 bar is within about 0.1 % of ideal; steam at 10 bar and 180 °C is not. The error grows with pressure and near saturation, so a result that comes from P V = n R T near the critical point should be checked against the compressibility chart.

3.4 • Ideal-gas processes: constant V, P, T, adiabatic and polytropic

Definition / principle

An ideal-gas process is a path on which one relation between P, V and T is maintained. Five are used: constant volume (isochoric), constant pressure (isobaric), constant temperature (isothermal), no heat transfer (adiabatic) and the general polytropic path P Vn = constant, of which the first four are special cases.

Detailed theory and conditions

The polytropic relation is the key to the whole topic. Putting n = 0 gives P = constant (isobaric), n = 1 gives P V = constant (isothermal, ideal gas), n = γ gives the adiabatic path and n → ∞ gives V = constant (isochoric). A single formula for the work, W = m R (T₁ − T₂)/(n − 1), therefore covers every case except the isothermal one, where the denominator vanishes and the logarithmic form must be used instead.

An adiabatic path is always steeper than an isothermal one through the same point, because γ > 1. That is why a gas cools as it expands adiabatically — the work comes out of its internal energy — and why a compressor gets hot. During the suction and discharge strokes of a real compressor the pressure falls and rises at nearly constant volume, which is why the indicator diagram has rounded ends rather than clean verticals.

Equations and notation

PVn=c
W=mRTlnV2V1
T2T1=(P2P1)γ−1γ
Q=mcv(T2−T1)γ−nγ−1

Key points and data

  • n = 0 isobaric, n = 1 isothermal, n = γ adiabatic, n = ∞ isochoric; real compression often has n ≈ 1.2–1.35.
  • Adiabatic: Q = 0, so W = −ΔU and the gas cools on expansion.
  • Isothermal: ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so W = Q.
  • Watch the sign: work done by the gas is positive; a compressor that consumes work reports W negative.

Qualification

The formula W = m R (T₁ − T₂)/(n − 1) fails as n → 1, where it becomes 0/0; use the logarithmic form there. It also assumes constant heat capacity over the temperature range, which is a poor assumption for a wide range and for gases such as CO₂.

3.5 • Adiabatic relation P V^γ = constant

Symbols, model and assumptions

Model: an ideal gas in a perfectly insulated cylinder, compressed reversibly and adiabatically. Assumptions: ideal gas with constant cv and cp, reversible path, no heat transfer (Q = 0), no change of kinetic or potential energy.

  1. Start from the first law for a closed system and set Q = 0 for an adiabatic path.

    −P dV=mcv dT

  2. Write the ideal-gas law for the same mass and differentiate it at constant mass.

    P dV+V dP=mR dT

  3. Eliminate dT between the two equations to get a relation between P and V alone.

    P dV+V dP=−RcvP dV

  4. Collect the P dV terms. Use R/c_v = γ − 1, which follows from c_p − c_v = R and γ = c_p/c_v.

    V dP=−γP dV

  5. Separate the variables so that P is with dP and V is with dV.

    dPP=−γdVV

  6. Integrate between states 1 and 2 with γ constant.

    lnP2P1=−γlnV2V1

  7. Take the exponential of both sides and rearrange to the standard form.

    PVγ=const

Result

PVγ=c
3.6 • Equations of state for real gases

Definition / principle

A real gas deviates from P V = n R T because its molecules have finite volume and attract one another. The deviation is measured by the compressibility factor Z = P V / n R T, which equals 1 for an ideal gas and departs from 1 as pressure rises or as the temperature approaches the critical temperature.

Detailed theory and conditions

Two corrections explain the shape of the Z curve. At moderate pressure the attraction between molecules pulls them closer than ideal, so the volume is smaller and Z falls below 1. At high pressure the molecules' own volume leaves less free space, so Z rises above 1. At very low pressure both effects vanish and Z → 1, which is why the ideal-gas law works so well near atmospheric conditions.

Three tools are used in practice. The Van der Waals equation (P + a/V²)(V − b) = R T applies the two corrections explicitly and is the basis of every later cubic equation. The virial equation Z = 1 + B/V + C/V² + … expands Z in powers of volume with experimentally fitted coefficients. The compressibility chart uses the principle of corresponding states: all gases obey nearly the same Z curve when plotted against reduced pressure and temperature, so one chart serves every gas.

Equations and notation

Z=PVnRT
(P+aV2)(V−b)=RT
Z=1+BV+CV2
a=27R2T2c64Pc

Key points and data

  • Van der Waals constants: a measures attraction (large for polar gases), b measures molecular volume.
  • Critical constants from a and b: Tc = 8a/(27Rb), Pc = a/(27b²), Vc = 3b.
  • Virial: B is the second virial coefficient, negative at low temperature (attraction dominates) and positive at high temperature.
  • Corresponding states: all gases have Z ≈ 1 when Tr is large, so the chart is used mainly for 0.8 < Tr < 3.

Qualification

The Van der Waals equation is qualitative, not accurate: it predicts the critical compressibility factor Zc = 3/8 = 0.375 for every gas, whereas real gases range from about 0.23 to 0.29. It is used to explain behaviour and to introduce cubic equations, not to size equipment.

Solved numericals and practicals
Ideal-gas law: volume of a gas at given conditions

Given

3 kmol of an ideal gas is held at 4 bar and 320 K. R = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K.

Find

The volume occupied by the gas.

Formula

V=nRTP

Substitution and calculation

P = 4 bar = 400 kPa. V = 3 × 8.314 × 320 / 400 = 7 981.4 / 400 = 19.95 m³.

Final answer with units

V = 19.95 m³ ≈ 20 m³.

Validity check

One kmol at 320 K and 4 bar should occupy about 22.4 × (320/273) × (1/4) ≈ 6.6 m³, so three kmol give about 20 m³ — the answer is the right order.

Adiabatic compression with the PV^γ relation

Given

2 kg of air at 1 bar and 300 K is compressed adiabatically and reversibly to 8 bar. γ = 1.4, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, c_v = 0.718 kJ/kg·K.

Find

Final temperature, work input and heat transfer.

Formula

T2=T1(P2P1)γ−1γ
W=mR(T1−T2)γ−1

Substitution and calculation

(γ−1)/γ = 0.2857. T₂ = 300 × 8^0.2857 = 300 × 1.811 = 543.3 K. W = 2 × 0.287 × (300 − 543.3)/0.4 = 0.574 × (−243.3)/0.4 = −349.1 kJ. The negative sign means 349.1 kJ of work is supplied.

Final answer with units

T₂ = 543 K; W = −349.1 kJ (work input); Q = 0; ΔU = +349.1 kJ.

Validity check

Check with ΔU: m c_v ΔT = 2 × 0.718 × 243.3 = 349.3 kJ, which matches the work within rounding — as it must, because Q = 0 means all the work becomes internal energy.

Compressibility factor and real volume

Given

Carbon dioxide at 310 K and 70 bar. Tc = 304.2 K, Pc = 73.8 bar. The compressibility chart gives Z ≈ 0.72 at these reduced conditions. R = 0.1889 kJ/kg·K.

Find

Reduced properties, Z, and the actual specific volume compared with the ideal value.

Formula

Tr=TTc
v=ZRTP

Substitution and calculation

T_r = 310/304.2 = 1.019; P_r = 70/73.8 = 0.949. Ideal volume: v_ideal = 0.1889 × 310/7 000 = 8.366 × 10⁻³ m³/kg. Actual: v = 0.72 × 8.366 × 10⁻³ = 6.02 × 10⁻³ m³/kg.

Final answer with units

T_r = 1.02, P_r = 0.95, Z = 0.72; v = 6.02 × 10⁻³ m³/kg, about 28 % below the ideal value.

Validity check

Tr ≈ 1 means the gas is close to its critical temperature, where Z is far from 1; had we used the ideal-gas law the volume would be over-estimated by 39 %. This is why CO₂ near 31 °C is a poor ideal gas but an excellent dense solvent.

Van der Waals equation for one mole

Given

One mole of a gas occupies 0.5 L at 300 K. For the gas, a = 3.592 bar·L²/mol² and b = 0.042 67 L/mol. R = 0.083 14 bar·L/mol·K.

Find

The pressure from the ideal-gas law and from the Van der Waals equation.

Formula

P=RTV
P=RTV−b−aV2

Substitution and calculation

Ideal: P = 0.083 14 × 300/0.5 = 49.88 bar. Van der Waals: V − b = 0.5 − 0.042 67 = 0.457 33 L. R T/(V − b) = 24.942/0.457 33 = 54.54 bar. a/V² = 3.592/0.25 = 14.37 bar. P = 54.54 − 14.37 = 40.17 bar.

Final answer with units

P_ideal = 49.9 bar; P_vdW = 40.2 bar — the ideal law over-predicts by about 24 %.

Validity check

The two corrections pull in opposite directions: the volume correction (V − b) raises the pressure, the attraction term (a/V²) lowers it, and here attraction wins. At this density the gas is far from ideal, which is the expected conclusion for half a litre per mole.

Polytropic compression of air

Given

1.5 kg of air is compressed from 1 bar, 290 K to 6 bar according to P V^1.25 = constant. R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, c_v = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, γ = 1.4.

Find

Final temperature, work input, heat transfer and the polytropic index check.

Formula

T2=T1(P2P1)n−1n
W=mR(T1−T2)n−1
Q=mcv(T2−T1)γ−nγ−1

Substitution and calculation

(n−1)/n = 0.25/1.25 = 0.2. T₂ = 290 × 6^0.2 = 290 × 1.431 = 415.0 K. W = 1.5 × 0.287 × (290 − 415)/0.25 = 0.4305 × (−125)/0.25 = −215.3 kJ. Q = 1.5 × 0.718 × 125 × (1.4 − 1.25)/0.4 = 1.077 × 125 × 0.375 = −50.5 kJ.

Final answer with units

T₂ = 415 K; work input = 215.3 kJ; heat rejected ≈ 50.5 kJ. Since 1 < n < γ, the gas is cooled during compression as well as compressed.

Validity check

Check with the first law: ΔU = m c_v ΔT = 1.5 × 0.718 × 125 = 134.6 kJ. Q − W = −50.5 − (−215.3) = 164.8 kJ, which should equal ΔU. The gap is rounding in c_v; use c_v = R/(γ − 1) = 0.7175 for exact agreement.

The P–V diagram of a pure substance

The five ideal-gas processes on a P–V diagram

RelationFormula and notes
Compressibility factorZ = P V / n R T; V = Z n R T / P
Read Z from the chart using Pr and Tr.
Reduced coordinatesP_r = P/P_c; T_r = T/T_c; V_r = V/V_c
Principle of corresponding states: all gases collapse onto one chart.
Van der Waals(P + a/V²)(V − b) = R T; Tc = 8a/(27Rb); Pc = a/(27b²)
Predicts Zc = 3/8 for every gas, so use it qualitatively.
VirialZ = 1 + B/V + C/V² + …

Viva questions
1. Explain PVT behaviour of a pure fluid and state how many properties fix its state.

PVT behaviour is the relation between pressure, volume and temperature. For a pure fluid in a single phase only two of the three are independent (F = 2), so fixing any two fixes the third through an equation of state or a table.

2. Draw and explain the P–V diagram of a pure substance.

Isotherms below Tc show a flat plateau where liquid and vapour coexist. The plateau shortens as T rises and vanishes at the critical point. Above Tc the isotherm is continuous — no phase change. The dome joins all plateau ends.

3. State the ideal-gas law and the conditions under which it applies.

P V = n R T. It applies at low pressure and high temperature, where molecular volume and intermolecular attraction are negligible. It fails near the critical point and near saturation.

4. What is a polytropic process? What do n = 0, 1, γ and ∞ represent?

A process following P V^n = constant. n = 0 is isobaric, n = 1 is isothermal, n = γ is adiabatic and n → ∞ is isochoric. Real compression usually has n between 1.2 and 1.35.

5. Why is an adiabatic curve steeper than an isothermal curve?

On an adiabatic path no heat enters, so the work comes out of internal energy and the temperature falls as the gas expands. The isothermal path keeps T constant by taking in heat. Since γ > 1 the adiabatic relation P V^γ = c falls faster than P V = c.

6. Define compressibility factor Z and explain why it can be less or greater than 1.

Z = P V / n R T. Below 1 when intermolecular attraction dominates and the volume is smaller than ideal; above 1 when molecular volume dominates at high pressure. Z → 1 as P → 0.

7. Write the Van der Waals equation and state the meaning of a and b.

(P + a/V²)(V − b) = R T. The constant a corrects for intermolecular attraction and b for the finite volume occupied by the molecules themselves.

8. What is the principle of corresponding states?

All gases obey nearly the same compressibility relation when expressed in reduced coordinates Pr = P/Pc and Tr = T/Tc. One generalised chart therefore serves every gas, which is why the compressibility chart is universal.
